The majority recited (wa-layalin 'ashrin) with tanwin, and Ibn 'Abbas with idafah (construct). Some vocalized it as (wa-layali 'ashrin) with the lam without the ya', and some (wa-layali 'ashrin) with the ya', meaning wa-layali ayyamin 'ashrin (and nights of ten days). Since the counted noun omitted is masculine, the ta' is dropped from 'ashr.

The majority recited (wal-watri) with fath on the waw and sukun on the ta', which is the dialect of Quraysh. Al-Aghurr reported it from Ibn 'Abbas, as did Abu Raja', Ibn Thabbat, Qatadah, Talhah, al-A'mash, and al-Hasan with a variant from him. Al-Akhawan (Hamzah and al-Kisa'i) recited it with kasr on the waw, which is the dialect of Tamim. Both dialects are used for the singular, but for the camel saddle only kasr is used. Al-Asma'i related both dialects for it, and Yunus reported from Abu 'Amr fath on the waw and kasr on the ta'.

The apparent meaning and the view of the majority, including 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn al-Zubayr, is that al-fajr is the well-known dawn, sworn by as the dawn is sworn by. It is meant as a genus, not the dawn of a specific day. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: it is the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). 'Ikrimah said: the Day of Friday. Al-Dahhak said: from Dhu al-Hijjah. Muqatil said: the night of Jam' (Muzdalifah). Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: from the first day of Muharram. It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas that al-fajr is the whole day. And from him and from Zayd ibn Aslam: al-fajr is the dawn prayer (salat al-subh), and its recitation is the recitation of dawn. It was also said: the fajr of springs from rocks and other things.

Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Kalbi, Qatadah, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and 'Atiyyah al-'Awfi said: the ten nights are the ten of Dhu al-Hijjah. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: the last ten nights of Ramadan. Ibn Jurayj said: the first of them (the first ten of Dhu al-Hijjah). Yaman and a group said: the first ten of Muharram, which includes the Day of 'Ashura'. Masruq and Mujahid said: the ten of Musa, peace be upon him, which God completed.

It was said: the more apparent view is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, because of the hadith agreed upon as sound. 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, said: "When the (last) ten entered, the Messenger of God would tighten his waist-wrapper, revive his night in worship, and wake his family." (ﷺ)

Al-Tabrizi said: they agreed that it refers to the last ten (nights) of Ramadan; no one disagreed about it, so its glorification is appropriate to the glorification of the oath.

Al-Zamakhshari said: by the ten nights he meant the ten of Dhu al-Hijjah. If you ask: why are they indefinite (munakkarah) among what is sworn by? I say: because they are specific nights from among the genus of nights; the ten are a part of them, or they are specified by a virtue that others do not have. If you ask: why were they not defined with the lam of prior reference (lam al-'ahd), since they are known and familiar nights? I say: if that were done, they would not stand alone with the meaning of virtue that is in the indefinite form, and because it is better for the lams to be homogeneous, so that the speech is further from obscurity and enigma. End of his words.

As for the two questions, they are obvious. As for the answer to them, it is a patched-together expression from which no meaning can be understood, so it is either accepted or rejected.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 89, verses 3–14:**

﴿By the even and the odd﴾: He mentioned thirty-six opinions about them in the book *al-Tahrir wa al-Tahbir*. We grew weary of reciting them, let alone writing them down in this book of ours. It is related from Imran ibn Husayn, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "(They are the prayers: among them is the even and among them is the odd.)" Abu Ayyub related from him: "(The even is the Day of Arafah and the Day of Eid al-Adha, and the odd is the Night of Sacrifice.)" Jabir related from him ﷺ: "(The even is the Day of Sacrifice, and the odd is the Day of Arafah.)" In this hadith there is an explanation by him, upon him be prayer and peace, of the dawn as the morning, and of the ten nights as the ten days of sacrifice. This is the opinion of Ibn Abbas and Ikrimah. Al-Nahhas preferred it and said: the hadith of Abu al-Zubayr from Jabir is what is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ, and it is more sound in its chain (isnad) than the hadith of Imran ibn Husayn: "(Fasting the Day of Arafah is odd, because it is the ninth of them, and the Day of Sacrifice is even, because it is the tenth of them.)" Ibn Atiyyah mentioned fourteen opinions concerning the even and the odd, and al-Zamakhshari mentioned three. Then he said: "They have indeed multiplied the opinions about the even and the odd, to the point that they nearly exhausted all the kinds of things to which these two may apply, and that is of little benefit and deserves to be neglected." End of quotation.

﴿And the night when it passes﴾: This is an oath by the genus of the night. *Yasri* means it goes away and comes to an end, like His saying: ﴿And the night when it turns back﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:33]. Al-Akhfash and Ibn Qutaybah said: *yasri fihi* (travels in it), so it is of the type of *layluka na'im* (your night is sleeping). Mujahid, Ikrimah and al-Kalbi said: what is meant is the Night of Jam' (Muzdalifah), because one travels in it. The answer to the oath is omitted. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is "Surely He will punish," indicated by His saying: "Have you not seen" up to His saying: ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: the answer is ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾. Ibn al-Zubayr read *bi-ʿAdi* in construct, and *Arama* with a fatha on the hamzah and a kasrah on the ra', which is a dialect for the city. Al-Dahhak read *bi-ʿAdin* with tanwin, and also *bi-ʿAdin* without tanwin, and *Aram* with a fatha on the hamzah and a sukun on the ra' as a lightened form of *Aramm*, with a kasrah on the ra'. If it is a tribe, it is correct to attach ʿAd to it and to separate it from it as a substitute or an appositive. If it is a city, the attachment to it is evident, and the separation in it would be through an omitted modifier, i.e., ʿAd, people of Iram, possessors of pillars.

It was also read: *Irami dhati* with the attachment of Iram to *dhat*, and *al-Iram* means the landmark, meaning: ʿAd, the landmarks of the possessor of pillars. And whoever reads *Arramma* as a past verb with *dhata* in the accusative means: God made the possessor of pillars into dust (*rameem*). *Arramma* would be a substitute for ﴿your Lord did﴾ and an explanation of *fa'ala*. If ﴿possessors of pillars﴾ is an attribute of the tribe, Ibn Abbas said: it is a metaphor for the length of their bodies, and from this it is said: *rafiʿ al-ʿimad* (of high pillar), their statures being likened to pillars, and from it their saying: *rajulun ʿamad* and *ʿumdan*, i.e., tall. Ikrimah and Muqatil said: the pillars of their houses with which they used to travel, for they were people of the tent-pole. Ibn Zayd said: the pillars of their structures. If it is an attribute of the city, then the pillars are of the stones with which it was built. It was also said: the lofty palaces and towers are called *ʿimad*. It is related from Mujahid: *aram*, a verbal noun from *aRima yaʾramu* when he perished, and the meaning is: like the perishing of the possessors of pillars. This is a strange opinion. It is as if the meaning of ﴿How did your Lord deal with ʿAd﴾ is: how did He destroy ʿAd like the destruction of the possessors of pillars? The exegetes mentioned that the possessors of pillars was a city which Shaddad ibn ʿAd built when he heard the mention of Paradise with descriptions that it was extremely distant or practically impossible to be built on earth like it. God sent upon it and upon its people a cry before they entered it, and they all perished. Its story can be consulted in *al-Tahrir*, and some of it is in *al-Kashshaf*.

The majority read ﴿was not created﴾ in the passive voice with *mithluha* in the nominative. Ibn al-Zubayr read it in the active voice with *mithlaha* in the accusative. It is also related from him: *nakhluq* with a nun, and the pronoun in *mithlaha* refers to the city which is the possessor of pillars in the lands, i.e., in the lands of this world, or it refers to the tribe, i.e., in the greatness of bodies and strength. Ibn Wathhab read *wa-Thamudin* with tanwin. The majority read it not taking tanwin.

﴿Who hewed the rock﴾: they cut through it and carved it, and made houses from the stones in it, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and you hew out of the mountains﴾ [al-Shuʿara 26:149], houses. It is said: the first to carve out mountains, rocks and marble were Thamud, and they built seven hundred and thousand cities, all of stone, in the valley, the Valley of al-Qura. It is also said: they cut through their valley and brought their water through a rock they split, the deed of one of strength and of hopes. ﴿Possessor of stakes﴾: the discussion of this has preceded in Surah Sad. ﴿Who﴾ is an attribute of ʿAd, Thamud and Pharaoh, or it is in the accusative as a term of blame, or in the nominative by supposing "they." ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾: He left the matter vague here and clarified it in al-Haqqah and elsewhere. It is said: he poured the whip upon him, covered him and enveloped him. The verb *sabba* was used because it implies rapidity in descending upon the one struck. The poet said:

*So he poured upon them blinding (fine) ones, as if they were downpours that are not from a cloud nor a drop.*

He means those who were punished with the hadd in the story of the slander. Some later poets said, describing a rope:

*We poured upon them, as wrongdoers, devils, and then there flew with them swift hands and feet.*

He specified the whip and so it was borrowed for punishment, because it requires of repetition and recurrence what the sword and other instruments do not require. Al-Zamakhshari said: He mentioned the whip as an indication that what He inflicted upon them in this world of great punishment, compared with what He prepared for them in the Hereafter, is like the whip when compared with all other means by which one is punished. *Al-Mirsad* and *al-Marsad* are the place in which watching takes place; it is a *mif'al* form from *rasadahu*. This is a parable for His watching over the disobedient with punishment, and that they cannot escape Him. Ibn Atiyyah said: it may be that *al-mirsad* in the verse is an active participle, as if He said: *la-bi-l-rasid* (indeed the watcher), and He expressed it with the intensive pattern. End of quotation. Had it been as he claimed, the *ba'* would not enter, because it is not in a place where it could enter, neither as an extra particle nor as a non-extra one.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 89, verses 3–14:**

﴿By the even and the odd﴾: He mentioned thirty-six opinions about them in the book *al-Tahrir wa al-Tahbir*. We grew weary of reciting them, let alone writing them down in this book of ours. It is related from Imran ibn Husayn, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "(They are the prayers: among them is the even and among them is the odd.)" Abu Ayyub related from him: "(The even is the Day of Arafah and the Day of Eid al-Adha, and the odd is the Night of Sacrifice.)" Jabir related from him ﷺ: "(The even is the Day of Sacrifice, and the odd is the Day of Arafah.)" In this hadith there is an explanation by him, upon him be prayer and peace, of the dawn as the morning, and of the ten nights as the ten days of sacrifice. This is the opinion of Ibn Abbas and Ikrimah. Al-Nahhas preferred it and said: the hadith of Abu al-Zubayr from Jabir is what is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ, and it is more sound in its chain (isnad) than the hadith of Imran ibn Husayn: "(Fasting the Day of Arafah is odd, because it is the ninth of them, and the Day of Sacrifice is even, because it is the tenth of them.)" Ibn Atiyyah mentioned fourteen opinions concerning the even and the odd, and al-Zamakhshari mentioned three. Then he said: "They have indeed multiplied the opinions about the even and the odd, to the point that they nearly exhausted all the kinds of things to which these two may apply, and that is of little benefit and deserves to be neglected." End of quotation.

﴿And the night when it passes﴾: This is an oath by the genus of the night. *Yasri* means it goes away and comes to an end, like His saying: ﴿And the night when it turns back﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:33]. Al-Akhfash and Ibn Qutaybah said: *yasri fihi* (travels in it), so it is of the type of *layluka na'im* (your night is sleeping). Mujahid, Ikrimah and al-Kalbi said: what is meant is the Night of Jam' (Muzdalifah), because one travels in it. The answer to the oath is omitted. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is "Surely He will punish," indicated by His saying: "Have you not seen" up to His saying: ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: the answer is ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾. What appears to be the case is that the answer is omitted and is indicated by what precedes it from the end of Surah al-Ghashiyah, namely His saying: ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return; then indeed, upon Us is their reckoning﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 88:25–26]. Its estimated form is: "Surely their return is to Us and their reckoning is upon Us." As for the saying of Muqatil: "Hal" is here in a position whose estimated form is: "Indeed in that is an oath for one of understanding" — this opinion does not come from careful consideration. This is because, if the construction were "Indeed in that is an oath for one of understanding," the thing sworn to would not be mentioned, and there would remain an oath with no thing sworn to, since what he estimated, namely that in that is an oath for one of understanding, cannot be the thing sworn to. And "hal fi dhalika" (is there in that) is a confirmation of the greatness of these oaths, i.e., is there in them a sufficient oath for one of intellect, so that he may be restrained and reflect upon the signs of God? Then the first of them were called "the First ʿAd," and Iram is a relative noun derived from their forefather's name. The later ones were called "the Last ʿAd." Mujahid and Qatadah said: it is a specific tribe. Ibn Ishaq said: Iram is the father of all of ʿAd.

The majority said: Iram is a great city belonging to them, which was in Yemen, unrivalled upon the face of the earth. Muhammad ibn Kab said: it is Alexandria. ﴿As for man﴾: He, the Exalted, mentioned what the Quraysh used to say and what they inferred from it about Allah's honouring or humiliating His servant. They would regard the one honoured as the one who possesses wealth and children, and the humiliated as the opposite. Since this view was prevalent among them, they were rebuked for it. ﴿Man (al-insan)﴾ is a noun of genus, and this attitude is found among many people of Islam. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "How is his saying ﴿As for man﴾ connected?" I say: it is connected to His saying, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [al-Fajr: 14]. It is as if He said: Allah, the Exalted, requires of man only obedience and striving for the final outcome, and He watches over the disobedient. ﴿As for man﴾, however, does not seek that, and is concerned only with the immediate life and what gives him pleasure and comfort in it. End of quote. In this statement there is an explicit declaration of the Mu'tazilite doctrine (madhhab al-i'tizal, the doctrine of the Mu'tazila), in his saying that He requires from man only obedience.

The word ﴿idha﴾ (when) is the governing element in this clause, with the intended meaning being deferred: ﴿fa-yaqulu﴾ (so he says) is then understood as a statement made at the time of the beginning, that is, "so he says such-and-such when." This ﴿fa﴾ does not prevent what follows it from governing what precedes it. Although it is a ﴿fa﴾ that entered the predicate of the subject because of ﴿amma﴾ (as for), which carries the sense of a condition. After the second ﴿amma﴾ there is an implied element, which creates the balance between the two sentences. Its estimated form is: ﴿fa-amma idha huwa ma ibtalahu﴾ (so as for when it is that He tested him), and ﴿fa-yaqulu﴾ is the predicate of that implied subject. ﴿Ibtalahu﴾ means He tested him: will he be thankful or ungrateful when He expands provision for him? Will he be patient or distressed when He restricts it for him? This is in accordance with His saying, ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya': 35].

He paired ﴿wa-na"amahu﴾ (and He granted him comfort) with His saying ﴿fa-qadara 'alayhi rizqahu﴾ (so He restricted his provision), but He did not pair ﴿fa-akramahu﴾ (so He honoured him) with the wording ﴿fa-ahanahu﴾ (so He humiliated him). This is because the one whose provision is restricted is not necessarily humiliated, since restriction of provision is considered humiliation only in that case. Do you not see that many people of righteousness have their provision restricted, such as the Imam Abu Sulayman Dawud ibn 'Ali al-Isfahani, may Allah be pleased with him, and others? Allah, the Exalted, censured the servant in both of these conditions.

As for His saying ﴿fa-yaqulu rabbi akraman﴾ (so he says: "My Lord has honoured me"), it is because this is a statement from him that he deserves honour and merits it. As for his saying ﴿ahanan﴾ (has humiliated me), it is because he called Allah's withholding of favour a humiliation, though it is not a humiliation. Alternatively, when He favours him, he acknowledges Allah's kindness to him, and when He does not favour him, he calls the withholding of Allah's favour a humiliation, not an acknowledgement in the saying ﴿akraman﴾ (has honoured me).

Ibn Kathir read ﴿akramani wa-ahanani﴾ with the ya' (the first person pronoun suffix) in both. Nafi' read it with the ya' when continuing and omitted it when pausing. Abu 'Amr allowed both options. The remaining seven readers omitted it in both, whether continuing or pausing. Whoever omits it at a pause makes the nun sukun (vowelless). The majority read ﴿fa-qadara﴾ with a light dal, while Abu Ja'far, 'Isa, Khalid, al-Hasan (with a variant from him), and Ibn 'Amir read it with a shadda (emphatic doubling) on the dal. The majority said: both have the same meaning, namely "restricted", and the doubling in it is for emphasis, not for transitivity. The saying of the human being ﴿ahanan﴾ does not necessarily follow from this, because giving what suffices is not a humiliation in it.

﴿Kalla﴾ (No!) is a rejection of their saying and belief, meaning: Allah's honouring and His measuring out of provision do not have as their cause what you have mentioned. Rather, His honouring of the servant is His facilitating for him what leads to his piety, and His humiliating of him is His facilitating for him disobedience. Then He informed them of their evil deeds in which they were engaged.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Kalla﴾ is a rebuke to man for his saying. Then he said: rather, there is something worse than this saying here, which is that Allah honours them with abundance of wealth, yet they do not discharge in it what is incumbent upon them, such as honouring the orphan by attending to him and being kind to him, and urging their people to feed the poor. They consume it greedily like cattle and love wealth so intensely that they hoard it. End of quote.

It is reported in a hadith: "The house most beloved to Allah, the Exalted, is a house in which there is an honoured orphan."

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Abu Raja', Qatada, al-Jahdari and Abu 'Amr read ﴿yukrimuna, wa-la yahuddun, wa-ya'kulun, wa-yuhibbun﴾ with the third-person ya' in these forms. The remaining seven read them with the second-person ta' (you). Abu Ja'far, Shayba, the Kufans, and Ibn Miqsam read ﴿tahaddun﴾ with an opening ta' and alif, its original form being ﴿tatahaddun﴾ (you urge one another), which is the reading of al-A'mash. That is, one of you urges another. 'Abdullah or 'Alqama, Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak, and al-Shirazi from al-Kisa'i read it the same way, except that they put a damma on the ta', meaning ﴿tuhaddun﴾ (you urge), that is, you urge yourselves, that is, one another. The form tafa"ala and fa"ala also come with the same meaning.

﴿'ala ta'am﴾ (on the feeding of) may mean ﴿it'am﴾ (feeding), like ﴿'ata'﴾ (giving) meaning ﴿i'ta'﴾ (giving). The better interpretation is that there is an omitted noun before it, meaning: on the bestowal of food.

﴿And you devour the inheritance﴾: They did not bequeath inheritance to women or to young children. They consumed their share and said: "None takes the inheritance except one who fights and protects the territory." The word ﴿turath﴾ (inheritance) has a ta' that replaces a waw, as in ﴿tukla﴾ and ﴿tukhama﴾ from ﴿tawakkaltu﴾ and ﴿wakhimtu﴾. It was also said: they consumed what the deceased had gathered through wrongdoing, while knowing this, combining the lawful and the unlawful, and wasting what they had inherited in spending, because they had not toiled to obtain it, just as we have witnessed idle heirs.

﴿Kalla﴾ is a rebuke to them for that and a denunciation of their action. Then He proceeded to threaten them and mentioned their regret over what they had neglected in the abode of this world.

﴿Dakkan dakkan﴾ (crushed, crushed) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), like their saying "baban baban" (door after door), meaning that the crushing is repeated upon them.

﴿And your Lord comes﴾: Al-Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: its meaning is that He becomes manifest to the creation at that time, and it is not a coming in the sense of motion. Likewise is the coming of the Overwhelming Calamity (al-tamma) and the Deafening Blast (al-sakhkha). It was also said: it means that His power and authority come. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an illustration of the manifestation of the signs of His dominion and the clarification of the effects of His power and authority. His state in this is represented by the state of a king who, when he comes in person, manifests through his presence from the traces of awe and governance what is not manifested by the presence of all his armies, ministers, and close companions. End of quote.

The word ﴿malik﴾ (king) is a noun of genus that includes the angels. It is related that they are the angels of each heaven, who will be in rows around the earth on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿rows upon rows﴾ (saffan saffan): the angels of each heaven descend and line up row after row, encircling the jinn and humankind. End of quote.

﴿And Hell is brought forth on that Day﴾, like His saying: ﴿And Hell is made apparent to whoever sees﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 36]. ﴿Yawma'idhin﴾ (on that Day) is a substitute for ﴿idha﴾ (when). Al-Zamakhshari said: the governing element of the accusative in both of them is ﴿yatadhakkaru﴾ (he will remember). End of quote. The apparent meaning of his statement is that the governing element of the substitute is the same as the governing element of what it substitutes, and this view has been attributed to Sibawayh. The well-known opinion is otherwise: the substitute is intended as a repetition of the governing element, meaning: he will remember what he neglected.

﴿And how can he have the reminder?﴾ means: how will remembrance benefit him? Because it is a time when remembrance will not benefit him. Had he admonished himself in this world, that would have benefited him in the Hereafter. This is the view of the majority. Al-Zamakhshari and others said: or it means the time of my life in this world, just as you say: "I came for sunrise" and "for such-and-such a date." Some said: it means for my life in my grave, meaning the one about which I used to deny. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is the clearest proof that choice was in their hands and dependent on their intention and will, and that they were not restrained from acts of obedience nor compelled to acts of disobedience, as the doctrine of the people of desires and innovations holds. Otherwise, what would be the meaning of regret? End of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila.

The majority read ﴿la yu'adhdhibu﴾ and ﴿la yuthiqu﴾ in the active voice, and the pronoun in ﴿'adhabahu﴾ (His punishment) and ﴿wuthaqahu﴾ (His bonds) refers to Allah, the Exalted, meaning that He does not entrust His punishment or His bonds to anyone, because the command in that matter belongs to Allah alone. Or it is from the severity of a sphere in which no one has ever been punished in this world like this. The first is clearer (p-471) in view of the saying ﴿la yu'adhdhibu, wa-la yuthiqu﴾. ﴿La﴾ (no) followed by the imperfect does not apply to the past except by a remote metaphor; rather, the imperfect after ﴿la﴾ is in its nature future. His state in this is represented by the state of a king who, when he comes in person, manifests through his presence from the traces of awe and governance what is not manifested by the presence of all his armies, ministers, and close companions. End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿rows upon rows﴾ (saffan saffan): the angels of each heaven descend and line up row after row, encircling the jinn and humankind. End of quote.

The well-known opinion is otherwise: the substitute is intended as a repetition of the governing element, meaning: he will remember what he neglected.

﴿And how can he have the reminder?﴾ means: how will remembrance benefit him? Because it is a time when remembrance will not benefit him. Al-Zamakhshari and others said: or it means the time of my life in this world, just as you say: "I came for sunrise" and "for such-and-such a date." Some said: it means for my life in my grave, meaning the one about which I used to deny. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is the clearest proof that choice was in their hands and dependent on their intention and will, and that they were not restrained from acts of obedience nor compelled to acts of disobedience, as the doctrine of the people of desires and innovations holds. Otherwise, what would be the meaning of regret? End of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an illustration of the manifestation of the signs of His dominion and the clarification of the effects of His power and authority. His state in this is represented by the state of a king who, when he comes in person, manifests through his presence from the traces of awe and governance what is not manifested by the presence of all his armies, ministers, and close companions. End of quote.

The word ﴿malik﴾ (king) is a noun of genus that includes the angels. It is related that they are the angels of each heaven, who will be in rows around the earth on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿rows upon rows﴾ (saffan saffan): the angels of each heaven descend and line up row after row, encircling the jinn and humankind. End of quote.

﴿And Hell is brought forth on that Day﴾, like His saying: ﴿And Hell is made apparent to whoever sees﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 36]. ﴿Yawma'idhin﴾ (on that Day) is a substitute for ﴿idha﴾ (when). Al-Zamakhshari said: the governing element of the accusative in both of them is ﴿yatadhakkaru﴾ (he will remember). End of quote. The apparent meaning of his statement is that the governing element of the substitute is the same as the governing element of what it substitutes, and this view has been attributed to Sibawayh. The well-known opinion is otherwise: the substitute is intended as a repetition of the governing element, meaning: he will remember what he neglected.

﴿And how can he have the reminder?﴾ means: how will remembrance benefit him? Because it is a time when remembrance will not benefit him. Had he admonished himself in this world, that would have benefited him in the Hereafter. This is the view of the majority. Al-Zamakhshari and others said: or it means the time of my life in this world, just as you say: "I came for sunrise" and "for such-and-such a date." Some said: it means for my life in my grave, meaning the one about which I used to deny. It is also possible that the pronoun before it refers to the disbeliever, meaning: none of the angels of punishment punishes as they punish him. It was also said: it refers to Allah, meaning: no one in this world punishes with the punishment of Allah upon the disbeliever. In this case the pronoun may be the object of the passive, which is the more apparent: meaning, no one is punished like His punishment, and no one is bound with chains and shackles like His bonds. Or: no one bears the punishment of the human being, in accordance with His saying: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. ﴿'Adhab﴾ (punishment) is placed in the position of ﴿ta'dhib﴾ (punishing). There is disagreement about borrowing such a form, namely a term used for something other than the verbal noun, like ﴿'ata'﴾ (gift), ﴿thawab﴾ (reward), ﴿'adhab﴾ (punishment), and ﴿kalam﴾ (speech). The Basrans do not permit it and do not analogize it.

The one punished is the disbeliever in general. It was also said: he is Umayya ibn Khalaf. It was also said: Ubayy ibn Khalaf. Ibn Zayd said: it is said to her at the time of death and her departure from the body of the believer in this world. It was also said: at the time of resurrection. It was also said: at the time of entering Paradise.

When He mentioned the state of the disbelievers, He said: O believers, persist and strive until you return pleased and well-pleasing. ﴿Radiyah﴾ (pleased) with what you have been given, ﴿mardiyyah﴾ (well-pleasing) in the sight of Allah.

It was also said: there is an omission, and it addressed the soul in the singular, saying: "enter into My servant," meaning: into the body of My servant. The verb ﴿fa-udkhuli﴾ is transitive first with ﴿fi﴾ and second without a preposition. This is because, when the object of entering is not a real place, it is transitive with ﴿fi﴾: you enter into a matter and enter into the crowd of people. From this is His saying ﴿fa-udkhuli fi 'ibadi﴾. When the object of entering is a real place, it is generally transitive without the mediation of ﴿fi﴾.

It was said that this was revealed concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, and it was said concerning Hamza, and it was said concerning Khubayb ibn 'Adi, may Allah be pleased with them all.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "How is his saying ﴿As for man﴾ connected?" I say: it is connected to His saying, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [al-Fajr: 14]. It is as if He said: Allah, the Exalted, requires of man only obedience and striving for the final outcome, and He watches over the disobedient. ﴿As for man﴾, however, does not seek that, and is concerned only with the immediate life and what gives him pleasure and comfort in it. End of quote. After the second ﴿amma﴾ there is an implied element, which creates the balance between the two sentences. Its estimated form is: ﴿fa-amma idha huwa ma ibtalahu﴾ (so as for when it is that He tested him), and ﴿fa-yaqulu﴾ is the predicate of that implied subject. ﴿Ibtalahu﴾ means He tested him: will he be thankful or ungrateful when He expands provision for him? Do you not see that many people of righteousness have their provision restricted, such as the Imam Abu Sulayman Dawud ibn 'Ali al-Isfahani, may Allah be pleased with him, and others? Allah, the Exalted, censured the servant in both of these conditions.

As for his saying ﴿ahanan﴾ (has humiliated me), it is because he called Allah's withholding of favour a humiliation, though it is not a humiliation. Alternatively, when He favours him, he acknowledges Allah's kindness to him, and when He does not favour him, he calls the withholding of Allah's favour a humiliation, not an acknowledgement in the saying ﴿akraman﴾ (has honoured me).

Then He informed them of their evil deeds in which they were engaged.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Kalla﴾ is a rebuke to man for his saying. Then he said: rather, there is something worse than this saying here, which is that Allah honours them with abundance of wealth, yet they do not discharge in it what is incumbent upon them, such as honouring the orphan by attending to him and being kind to him, and urging their people to feed the poor. They consume it greedily like cattle and love wealth so intensely that they hoard it. End of quote.

It is reported in a hadith: "The house most beloved to Allah, the Exalted, is a house in which there is an honoured orphan."

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Abu Raja', Qatada, al-Jahdari and Abu 'Amr read ﴿yukrimuna, wa-la yahuddun, wa-ya'kulun, wa-yuhibbun﴾ with the third-person ya' in these forms. The form tafa"ala and fa"ala also come with the same meaning.

They consumed their share and said: "None takes the inheritance except one who fights and protects the territory." It was also said: they consumed what the deceased had gathered through wrongdoing, while knowing this, combining the lawful and the unlawful, and wasting what they had inherited in spending, because they had not toiled to obtain it, just as we have witnessed idle heirs.

﴿Kalla﴾ is a rebuke to them for that and a denunciation of their action. Then He proceeded to threaten them and mentioned their regret over what they had neglected in the abode of this world.

End of quote.

The majority read ﴿fi 'ibadi﴾ in the plural. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, al-Dahhak, Mujahid, Abu Ja'far, Abu Salih, al-Kalbi, Abu Shaykh al-Hana'i, and al-Yamani read ﴿fi 'abdi﴾ in the singular. The more apparent view is that the noun of genus is intended, so its meaning and the meaning of the plural are the same. It was also said: there is an omission, and it addressed the soul in the singular, saying: "enter into My servant," meaning: into the body of My servant. The verb ﴿fa-udkhuli﴾ is transitive first with ﴿fi﴾ and second without a preposition. This is because, when the object of entering is not a real place, it is transitive with ﴿fi﴾: you enter into a matter and enter into the crowd of people. From this is His saying ﴿fa-udkhuli fi 'ibadi﴾. When the object of entering is a real place, it is generally transitive without the mediation of ﴿fi﴾.

It was said that this was revealed concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, and it was said concerning Hamza, and it was said concerning Khubayb ibn 'Adi, may Allah be pleased with them all.

﴿As for man﴾: He, the Exalted, mentioned what the Quraysh used to say and what they inferred from it about Allah's honouring or humiliating His servant. They would regard the one honoured as the one who possesses wealth and children, and the humiliated as the opposite. Since this view was prevalent among them, they were rebuked for it. ﴿Man (al-insan)﴾ is a noun of genus, and this attitude is found among many people of Islam. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "How is his saying ﴿As for man﴾ connected?" I say: it is connected to His saying, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [al-Fajr: 14]. It is as if He said: Allah, the Exalted, requires of man only obedience and striving for the final outcome, and He watches over the disobedient. ﴿As for man﴾, however, does not seek that, and is concerned only with the immediate life and what gives him pleasure and comfort in it. End of quote. The word ﴿idha﴾ (when) is the governing element in this clause, with the intended meaning being deferred: ﴿fa-yaqulu﴾ (so he says) is then understood as a statement made at the time of the beginning, that is, "so he says such-and-such when." This ﴿fa﴾ does not prevent what follows it from governing what precedes it. Although it is a ﴿fa﴾ that entered the predicate of the subject because of ﴿amma﴾ (as for), which carries the sense of a condition. After the second ﴿amma﴾ there is an implied element, which creates the balance between the two sentences. Its estimated form is: ﴿fa-amma idha huwa ma ibtalahu﴾ (so as for when it is that He tested him), and ﴿fa-yaqulu﴾ is the predicate of that implied subject. ﴿Ibtalahu﴾ means He tested him: will he be thankful or ungrateful when He expands provision for him? Do you not see that many people of righteousness have their provision restricted, such as the Imam Abu Sulayman Dawud ibn 'Ali al-Isfahani, may Allah be pleased with him, and others? Allah, the Exalted, censured the servant in both of these conditions.

As for His saying ﴿fa-yaqulu rabbi akraman﴾ (so he says: "My Lord has honoured me"), it is because this is a statement from him that he deserves honour and merits it. As for his saying ﴿ahanan﴾ (has humiliated me), it is because he called Allah's withholding of favour a humiliation, though it is not a humiliation. Alternatively, when He favours him, he acknowledges Allah's kindness to him, and when He does not favour him, he calls the withholding of Allah's favour a humiliation, not an acknowledgement in the saying ﴿akraman﴾ (has honoured me).

Rather, His honouring of the servant is His facilitating for him what leads to his piety, and His humiliating of him is His facilitating for him disobedience. Then He informed them of their evil deeds in which they were engaged.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Kalla﴾ is a rebuke to man for his saying. Then he said: rather, there is something worse than this saying here, which is that Allah honours them with abundance of wealth, yet they do not discharge in it what is incumbent upon them, such as honouring the orphan by attending to him and being kind to him, and urging their people to feed the poor. They consume it greedily like cattle and love wealth so intensely that they hoard it. End of quote.

It is reported in a hadith: "The house most beloved to Allah, the Exalted, is a house in which there is an honoured orphan."

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Abu Raja', Qatada, al-Jahdari and Abu 'Amr read ﴿yukrimuna, wa-la yahuddun, wa-ya'kulun, wa-yuhibbun﴾ with the third-person ya' in these forms. Abu Ja'far, Shayba, the Kufans, and Ibn Miqsam read ﴿tahaddun﴾ with an opening ta' and alif, its original form being ﴿tatahaddun﴾ (you urge one another), which is the reading of al-A'mash. That is, one of you urges another. The form tafa"ala and fa"ala also come with the same meaning.

﴿And you devour the inheritance﴾: They did not bequeath inheritance to women or to young children. They consumed their share and said: "None takes the inheritance except one who fights and protects the territory." The word ﴿turath﴾ (inheritance) has a ta' that replaces a waw, as in ﴿tukla﴾ and ﴿tukhama﴾ from ﴿tawakkaltu﴾ and ﴿wakhimtu﴾. It was also said: they consumed what the deceased had gathered through wrongdoing, while knowing this, combining the lawful and the unlawful, and wasting what they had inherited in spending, because they had not toiled to obtain it, just as we have witnessed idle heirs.

﴿Kalla﴾ is a rebuke to them for that and a denunciation of their action. Then He proceeded to threaten them and mentioned their regret over what they had neglected in the abode of this world.

﴿Dakkan dakkan﴾ (crushed, crushed) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), like their saying "baban baban" (door after door), meaning that the crushing is repeated upon them.

Likewise is the coming of the Overwhelming Calamity (al-tamma) and the Deafening Blast (al-sakhkha). It was also said: it means that His power and authority come. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an illustration of the manifestation of the signs of His dominion and the clarification of the effects of His power and authority. His state in this is represented by the state of a king who, when he comes in person, manifests through his presence from the traces of awe and governance what is not manifested by the presence of all his armies, ministers, and close companions. End of quote.

There is disagreement about borrowing such a form, namely a term used for something other than the verbal noun, like ﴿'ata'﴾ (gift), ﴿thawab﴾ (reward), ﴿'adhab﴾ (punishment), and ﴿kalam﴾ (speech). The Basrans do not permit it and do not analogize it.

Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and Nafi', in one variant from them, read ﴿withaqahu﴾ with a kasra on the waw. The majority read it with a fatha.

The one punished is the disbeliever in general. It was also said: he is Umayya ibn Khalaf. It was also said: Ubayy ibn Khalaf. It was also said: the intended meaning is Iblis, and the evidence has been established that he is more severely punished than people. This view is refuted by His saying: ﴿On that Day the human being will remember﴾, and all the pronouns are directed toward him.

This address is apparently spoken by an angel. The majority read it with the feminine ta' (ya ayyatuha). Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿ya ayyuha﴾ without the ta'. I know of no one who said that it is masculine, even though the addressed noun is feminine, except the author of al-Badi'. This reading is evidence for that, and it has a basis in analogy: just as the dual and the plural are not inflected in the vocative, so the feminine is not inflected in the vocative of the feminine.

Ibn Zayd said: it is said to her at the time of death and her departure from the body of the believer in this world. It was also said: at the time of resurrection. It was also said: at the time of entering Paradise.

Al-Zamakhshari said: this is the clearest proof that choice was in their hands and dependent on their intention and will, and that they were not restrained from acts of obedience nor compelled to acts of disobedience, as the doctrine of the people of desires and innovations holds. Abu Ja'far, Shayba, the Kufans, and Ibn Miqsam read ﴿tahaddun﴾ with an opening ta' and alif, its original form being ﴿tatahaddun﴾ (you urge one another), which is the reading of al-A'mash. That is, one of you urges another. 'Abdullah or 'Alqama, Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak, and al-Shirazi from al-Kisa'i read it the same way, except that they put a damma on the ta', meaning ﴿tuhaddun﴾ (you urge), that is, you urge yourselves, that is, one another. The form tafa"ala and fa"ala also come with the same meaning.

﴿'ala ta'am﴾ (on the feeding of) may mean ﴿it'am﴾ (feeding), like ﴿'ata'﴾ (giving) meaning ﴿i'ta'﴾ (giving). The better interpretation is that there is an omitted noun before it, meaning: on the bestowal of food.

﴿And you devour the inheritance﴾: They did not bequeath inheritance to women or to young children. They consumed their share and said: "None takes the inheritance except one who fights and protects the territory." The word ﴿turath﴾ (inheritance) has a ta' that replaces a waw, as in ﴿tukla﴾ and ﴿tukhama﴾ from ﴿tawakkaltu﴾ and ﴿wakhimtu﴾. It was also said: they consumed what the deceased had gathered through wrongdoing, while knowing this, combining the lawful and the unlawful, and wasting what they had inherited in spending, because they had not toiled to obtain it, just as we have witnessed idle heirs.

﴿Kalla﴾ is a rebuke to them for that and a denunciation of their action. Then He proceeded to threaten them and mentioned their regret over what they had neglected in the abode of this world.

﴿Dakkan dakkan﴾ (crushed, crushed) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), like their saying "baban baban" (door after door), meaning that the crushing is repeated upon them.

﴿And your Lord comes﴾: Al-Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: its meaning is that He becomes manifest to the creation at that time, and it is not a coming in the sense of motion. Likewise is the coming of the Overwhelming Calamity (al-tamma) and the Deafening Blast (al-sakhkha). It was also said: it means that His power and authority come. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an illustration of the manifestation of the signs of His dominion and the clarification of the effects of His power and authority. His state in this is represented by the state of a king who, when he comes in person, manifests through his presence from the traces of awe and governance what is not manifested by the presence of all his armies, ministers, and close companions. End of quote.

The word ﴿malik﴾ (king) is a noun of genus that includes the angels. It is related that they are the angels of each heaven, who will be in rows around the earth on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿rows upon rows﴾ (saffan saffan): the angels of each heaven descend and line up row after row, encircling the jinn and humankind. End of quote.

﴿And Hell is brought forth on that Day﴾, like His saying: ﴿And Hell is made apparent to whoever sees﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 36]. ﴿Yawma'idhin﴾ (on that Day) is a substitute for ﴿idha﴾ (when). Al-Zamakhshari said: the governing element of the accusative in both of them is ﴿yatadhakkaru﴾ (he will remember). End of quote. The apparent meaning of his statement is that the governing element of the substitute is the same as the governing element of what it substitutes, and this view has been attributed to Sibawayh. The well-known opinion is otherwise: the substitute is intended as a repetition of the governing element, meaning: he will remember what he neglected.

﴿And how can he have the reminder?﴾ means: how will remembrance benefit him? Because it is a time when remembrance will not benefit him. Had he admonished himself in this world, that would have benefited him in the Hereafter. This is the view of the majority. Al-Zamakhshari and others said: or it means the time of my life in this world, just as you say: "I came for sunrise" and "for such-and-such a date." Some said: it means for my life in my grave, meaning the one about which I used to deny. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is the clearest proof that choice was in their hands and dependent on their intention and will, and that they were not restrained from acts of obedience nor compelled to acts of disobedience, as the doctrine of the people of desires and innovations holds. Otherwise, what would be the meaning of regret? End of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila.

The majority read ﴿la yu'adhdhibu﴾ and ﴿la yuthiqu﴾ in the active voice, and the pronoun in ﴿'adhabahu﴾ (His punishment) and ﴿wuthaqahu﴾ (His bonds) refers to Allah, the Exalted, meaning that He does not entrust His punishment or His bonds to anyone, because the command in that matter belongs to Allah alone. Or it is from the severity of a sphere in which no one has ever been punished in this world like this. The first is clearer (p-471) in view of the saying ﴿la yu'adhdhibu, wa-la yuthiqu﴾. ﴿La﴾ (no) followed by the imperfect does not apply to the past except by a remote metaphor; rather, the imperfect after ﴿la﴾ is in its nature future. It is also possible that the pronoun before it refers to the disbeliever, meaning: none of the angels of punishment punishes as they punish him. It was also said: it refers to Allah, meaning: no one in this world punishes with the punishment of Allah upon the disbeliever. This view is weakened by the fact that ﴿la yu'adhdhibu﴾ governs ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ (on that Day), which is a temporal adverb of the future.

Ibn Sirin, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Siwar al-Qadi, Abu Hayawa, Ibn Abi 'Abla, Abu Bahriyya, Salam, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub, and Sahl, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read ﴿yu'adhdhabu﴾ and ﴿yuthaqu﴾ with a fatha on the dhal and the tha', in the passive voice. In this case the pronoun may be the object of the passive, which is the more apparent: meaning, no one is punished like His punishment, and no one is bound with chains and shackles like His bonds. Or: no one bears the punishment of the human being, in accordance with His saying: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. ﴿'Adhab﴾ (punishment) is placed in the position of ﴿ta'dhib﴾ (punishing). There is disagreement about borrowing such a form, namely a term used for something other than the verbal noun, like ﴿'ata'﴾ (gift), ﴿thawab﴾ (reward), ﴿'adhab﴾ (punishment), and ﴿kalam﴾ (speech). The Basrans do not permit it and do not analogize it.

Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and Nafi', in one variant from them, read ﴿withaqahu﴾ with a kasra on the waw. The majority read it with a fatha.

The one punished is the disbeliever in general. It was also said: he is Umayya ibn Khalaf. It was also said: Ubayy ibn Khalaf. It was also said: the intended meaning is Iblis, and the evidence has been established that he is more severely punished than people. This view is refuted by His saying: ﴿On that Day the human being will remember﴾, and all the pronouns are directed toward him.

When He, the Exalted, mentioned some of the conditions of those who are punished, He mentioned some of the conditions of the believer, saying: ﴿O soul at rest﴾. This address is apparently spoken by an angel. The majority read it with the feminine ta' (ya ayyatuha). Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿ya ayyuha﴾ without the ta'. I know of no one who said that it is masculine, even though the addressed noun is feminine, except the author of al-Badi'. This reading is evidence for that, and it has a basis in analogy: just as the dual and the plural are not inflected in the vocative, so the feminine is not inflected in the vocative of the feminine.

﴿Al-mutma'innah﴾ (at rest) means the secure one, who is not touched by fear or grief. Or it means the one who was at rest in the truth, whose heart was not mixed with doubt. Ibn Zayd said: it is said to her at the time of death and her departure from the body of the believer in this world. It was also said: at the time of resurrection. It was also said: at the time of entering Paradise.

﴿Ila rabbiki﴾ (to your Lord) means: to the appointed meeting with your Lord. It was also said: the "Lord" here is the human being, not the soul, meaning: enter into the bodies. The soul is a noun of genus. It was also said: this address is now directed to the believers. When He mentioned the state of the disbelievers, He said: O believers, persist and strive until you return pleased and well-pleasing. ﴿Radiyah﴾ (pleased) with what you have been given, ﴿mardiyyah﴾ (well-pleasing) in the sight of Allah.

﴿Fa-udkhuli fi 'ibadi﴾ means: enter among My righteous servants. ﴿Wa-udkhuli jannati﴾ (and enter My Paradise) along with them. It was also said: the soul and the spirit are meant, and the meaning is: enter the bodies of My servants.

The majority read ﴿fi 'ibadi﴾ in the plural. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, al-Dahhak, Mujahid, Abu Ja'far, Abu Salih, al-Kalbi, Abu Shaykh al-Hana'i, and al-Yamani read ﴿fi 'abdi﴾ in the singular. The more apparent view is that the noun of genus is intended, so its meaning and the meaning of the plural are the same. It was also said: there is an omission, and it addressed the soul in the singular, saying: "enter into My servant," meaning: into the body of My servant. The verb ﴿fa-udkhuli﴾ is transitive first with ﴿fi﴾ and second without a preposition. This is because, when the object of entering is not a real place, it is transitive with ﴿fi﴾: you enter into a matter and enter into the crowd of people. From this is His saying ﴿fa-udkhuli fi 'ibadi﴾. When the object of entering is a real place, it is generally transitive without the mediation of ﴿fi﴾.

It was said that this was revealed concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, and it was said concerning Hamza, and it was said concerning Khubayb ibn 'Adi, may Allah be pleased with them all.

﴿As for man﴾: He, the Exalted, mentioned what the Quraysh used to say and what they inferred from it about Allah's honouring or humiliating His servant. They would regard the one honoured as the one who possesses wealth and children, and the humiliated as the opposite. Since this view was prevalent among them, they were rebuked for it. ﴿Man (al-insan)﴾ is a noun of genus, and this attitude is found among many people of Islam. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "How is his saying ﴿As for man﴾ connected?" I say: it is connected to His saying, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [al-Fajr: 14]. It is as if He said: Allah, the Exalted, requires of man only obedience and striving for the final outcome, and He watches over the disobedient. ﴿As for man﴾, however, does not seek that, and is concerned only with the immediate life and what gives him pleasure and comfort in it. End of quote. In this statement there is an explicit declaration of the Mu'tazilite doctrine (madhhab al-i'tizal, the doctrine of the Mu'tazila), in his saying that He requires from man only obedience.

The word ﴿idha﴾ (when) is the governing element in this clause, with the intended meaning being deferred: ﴿fa-yaqulu﴾ (so he says) is then understood as a statement made at the time of the beginning, that is, "so he says such-and-such when." This ﴿fa﴾ does not prevent what follows it from governing what precedes it. Although it is a ﴿fa﴾ that entered the predicate of the subject because of ﴿amma﴾ (as for), which carries the sense of a condition. After the second ﴿amma﴾ there is an implied element, which creates the balance between the two sentences. Its estimated form is: ﴿fa-amma idha huwa ma ibtalahu﴾ (so as for when it is that He tested him), and ﴿fa-yaqulu﴾ is the predicate of that implied subject. ﴿Ibtalahu﴾ means He tested him: will he be thankful or ungrateful when He expands provision for him? Will he be patient or distressed when He restricts it for him? This is in accordance with His saying, ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya': 35].

He paired ﴿wa-na"amahu﴾ (and He granted him comfort) with His saying ﴿fa-qadara 'alayhi rizqahu﴾ (so He restricted his provision), but He did not pair ﴿fa-akramahu﴾ (so He honoured him) with the wording ﴿fa-ahanahu﴾ (so He humiliated him). This is because the one whose provision is restricted is not necessarily humiliated, since restriction of provision is considered humiliation only in that case. Do you not see that many people of righteousness have their provision restricted, such as the Imam Abu Sulayman Dawud ibn 'Ali al-Isfahani, may Allah be pleased with him, and others? Allah, the Exalted, censured the servant in both of these conditions.

As for His saying ﴿fa-yaqulu rabbi akraman﴾ (so he says: "My Lord has honoured me"), it is because this is a statement from him that he deserves honour and merits it. As for his saying ﴿ahanan﴾ (has humiliated me), it is because he called Allah's withholding of favour a humiliation, though it is not a humiliation. Alternatively, when He favours him, he acknowledges Allah's kindness to him, and when He does not favour him, he calls the withholding of Allah's favour a humiliation, not an acknowledgement in the saying ﴿akraman﴾ (has honoured me).

Ibn Kathir read ﴿akramani wa-ahanani﴾ with the ya' (the first person pronoun suffix) in both. Nafi' read it with the ya' when continuing and omitted it when pausing. Abu 'Amr allowed both options. The remaining seven readers omitted it in both, whether continuing or pausing. Whoever omits it at a pause makes the nun sukun (vowelless). The majority read ﴿fa-qadara﴾ with a light dal, while Abu Ja'far, 'Isa, Khalid, al-Hasan (with a variant from him), and Ibn 'Amir read it with a shadda (emphatic doubling) on the dal. The majority said: both have the same meaning, namely "restricted", and the doubling in it is for emphasis, not for transitivity. The saying of the human being ﴿ahanan﴾ does not necessarily follow from this, because giving what suffices is not a humiliation in it.

﴿Kalla﴾ (No!) is a rejection of their saying and belief, meaning: Allah's honouring and His measuring out of provision do not have as their cause what you have mentioned. Rather, His honouring of the servant is His facilitating for him what leads to his piety, and His humiliating of him is His facilitating for him disobedience. Then He informed them of their evil deeds in which they were engaged.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Kalla﴾ is a rebuke to man for his saying. Then he said: rather, there is something worse than this saying here, which is that Allah honours them with abundance of wealth, yet they do not discharge in it what is incumbent upon them, such as honouring the orphan by attending to him and being kind to him, and urging their people to feed the poor. They consume it greedily like cattle and love wealth so intensely that they hoard it. End of quote.

It is reported in a hadith: "The house most beloved to Allah, the Exalted, is a house in which there is an honoured orphan."

Will he be patient or distressed when He restricts it for him? This is in accordance with His saying, ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya': 35].

He paired ﴿wa-na"amahu﴾ (and He granted him comfort) with His saying ﴿fa-qadara 'alayhi rizqahu﴾ (so He restricted his provision), but He did not pair ﴿fa-akramahu﴾ (so He honoured him) with the wording ﴿fa-ahanahu﴾ (so He humiliated him). This is because the one whose provision is restricted is not necessarily humiliated, since restriction of provision is considered humiliation only in that case. Do you not see that many people of righteousness have their provision restricted, such as the Imam Abu Sulayman Dawud ibn 'Ali al-Isfahani, may Allah be pleased with him, and others? Allah, the Exalted, censured the servant in both of these conditions.

As for His saying ﴿fa-yaqulu rabbi akraman﴾ (so he says: "My Lord has honoured me"), it is because this is a statement from him that he deserves honour and merits it. As for his saying ﴿ahanan﴾ (has humiliated me), it is because he called Allah's withholding of favour a humiliation, though it is not a humiliation. Alternatively, when He favours him, he acknowledges Allah's kindness to him, and when He does not favour him, he calls the withholding of Allah's favour a humiliation, not an acknowledgement in the saying ﴿akraman﴾ (has honoured me).

Ibn Kathir read ﴿akramani wa-ahanani﴾ with the ya' (the first person pronoun suffix) in both. Nafi' read it with the ya' when continuing and omitted it when pausing. Abu 'Amr allowed both options. The remaining seven readers omitted it in both, whether continuing or pausing. Whoever omits it at a pause makes the nun sukun (vowelless). The majority read ﴿fa-qadara﴾ with a light dal, while Abu Ja'far, 'Isa, Khalid, al-Hasan (with a variant from him), and Ibn 'Amir read it with a shadda (emphatic doubling) on the dal. The majority said: both have the same meaning, namely "restricted", and the doubling in it is for emphasis, not for transitivity. The saying of the human being ﴿ahanan﴾ does not necessarily follow from this, because giving what suffices is not a humiliation in it.

﴿Kalla﴾ (No!) is a rejection of their saying and belief, meaning: Allah's honouring and His measuring out of provision do not have as their cause what you have mentioned. Rather, His honouring of the servant is His facilitating for him what leads to his piety, and His humiliating of him is His facilitating for him disobedience. Then He informed them of their evil deeds in which they were engaged.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Kalla﴾ is a rebuke to man for his saying. Then he said: rather, there is something worse than this saying here, which is that Allah honours them with abundance of wealth, yet they do not discharge in it what is incumbent upon them, such as honouring the orphan by attending to him and being kind to him, and urging their people to feed the poor. They consume it greedily like cattle and love wealth so intensely that they hoard it. End of quote.

It is reported in a hadith: "The house most beloved to Allah, the Exalted, is a house in which there is an honoured orphan."

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Abu Raja', Qatada, al-Jahdari and Abu 'Amr read ﴿yukrimuna, wa-la yahuddun, wa-ya'kulun, wa-yuhibbun﴾ with the third-person ya' in these forms. The remaining seven read them with the second-person ta' (you). Abu Ja'far, Shayba, the Kufans, and Ibn Miqsam read ﴿tahaddun﴾ with an opening ta' and alif, its original form being ﴿tatahaddun﴾ (you urge one another), which is the reading of al-A'mash. That is, one of you urges another. 'Abdullah or 'Alqama, Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak, and al-Shirazi from al-Kisa'i read it the same way, except that they put a damma on the ta', meaning ﴿tuhaddun﴾ (you urge), that is, you urge yourselves, that is, one another. The form tafa"ala and fa"ala also come with the same meaning.

﴿'ala ta'am﴾ (on the feeding of) may mean ﴿it'am﴾ (feeding), like ﴿'ata'﴾ (giving) meaning ﴿i'ta'﴾ (giving). The better interpretation is that there is an omitted noun before it, meaning: on the bestowal of food.

﴿And you devour the inheritance﴾: They did not bequeath inheritance to women or to young children. They consumed their share and said: "None takes the inheritance except one who fights and protects the territory." The word ﴿turath﴾ (inheritance) has a ta' that replaces a waw, as in ﴿tukla﴾ and ﴿tukhama﴾ from ﴿tawakkaltu﴾ and ﴿wakhimtu﴾. It was also said: they consumed what the deceased had gathered through wrongdoing, while knowing this, combining the lawful and the unlawful, and wasting what they had inherited in spending, because they had not toiled to obtain it, just as we have witnessed idle heirs.

﴿Kalla﴾ is a rebuke to them for that and a denunciation of their action. Then He proceeded to threaten them and mentioned their regret over what they had neglected in the abode of this world.

﴿Dakkan dakkan﴾ (crushed, crushed) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), like their saying "baban baban" (door after door), meaning that the crushing is repeated upon them.

﴿And your Lord comes﴾: Al-Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: its meaning is that He becomes manifest to the creation at that time, and it is not a coming in the sense of motion. Likewise is the coming of the Overwhelming Calamity (al-tamma) and the Deafening Blast (al-sakhkha). It was also said: it means that His power and authority come. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an illustration of the manifestation of the signs of His dominion and the clarification of the effects of His power and authority. His state in this is represented by the state of a king who, when he comes in person, manifests through his presence from the traces of awe and governance what is not manifested by the presence of all his armies, ministers, and close companions. End of quote.

The word ﴿malik﴾ (king) is a noun of genus that includes the angels. It is related that they are the angels of each heaven, who will be in rows around the earth on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿rows upon rows﴾ (saffan saffan): the angels of each heaven descend and line up row after row, encircling the jinn and humankind. End of quote.

﴿And Hell is brought forth on that Day﴾, like His saying: ﴿And Hell is made apparent to whoever sees﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 36]. ﴿Yawma'idhin﴾ (on that Day) is a substitute for ﴿idha﴾ (when). Al-Zamakhshari said: the governing element of the accusative in both of them is ﴿yatadhakkaru﴾ (he will remember). End of quote. The apparent meaning of his statement is that the governing element of the substitute is the same as the governing element of what it substitutes, and this view has been attributed to Sibawayh. The well-known opinion is otherwise: the substitute is intended as a repetition of the governing element, meaning: he will remember what he neglected.

﴿And how can he have the reminder?﴾ means: how will remembrance benefit him? Because it is a time when remembrance will not benefit him. Had he admonished himself in this world, that would have benefited him in the Hereafter. This is the view of the majority. Al-Zamakhshari and others said: or it means the time of my life in this world, just as you say: "I came for sunrise" and "for such-and-such a date." Some said: it means for my life in my grave, meaning the one about which I used to deny. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is the clearest proof that choice was in their hands and dependent on their intention and will, and that they were not restrained from acts of obedience nor compelled to acts of disobedience, as the doctrine of the people of desires and innovations holds. Otherwise, what would be the meaning of regret? End of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila.

The majority read ﴿la yu'adhdhibu﴾ and ﴿la yuthiqu﴾ in the active voice, and the pronoun in ﴿'adhabahu﴾ (His punishment) and ﴿wuthaqahu﴾ (His bonds) refers to Allah, the Exalted, meaning that He does not entrust His punishment or His bonds to anyone, because the command in that matter belongs to Allah alone. Or it is from the severity of a sphere in which no one has ever been punished in this world like this. The first is clearer (p-471) in view of the saying ﴿la yu'adhdhibu, wa-la yuthiqu﴾. ﴿La﴾ (no) followed by the imperfect does not apply to the past except by a remote metaphor; rather, the imperfect after ﴿la﴾ is in its nature future. It is also possible that the pronoun before it refers to the disbeliever, meaning: none of the angels of punishment punishes as they punish him. It was also said: it refers to Allah, meaning: no one in this world punishes with the punishment of Allah upon the disbeliever. This view is weakened by the fact that ﴿la yu'adhdhibu﴾ governs ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ (on that Day), which is a temporal adverb of the future.

Ibn Sirin, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Siwar al-Qadi, Abu Hayawa, Ibn Abi 'Abla, Abu Bahriyya, Salam, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub, and Sahl, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read ﴿yu'adhdhabu﴾ and ﴿yuthaqu﴾ with a fatha on the dhal and the tha', in the passive voice. In this case the pronoun may be the object of the passive, which is the more apparent: meaning, no one is punished like His punishment, and no one is bound with chains and shackles like His bonds. Or: no one bears the punishment of the human being, in accordance with His saying: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. ﴿'Adhab﴾ (punishment) is placed in the position of ﴿ta'dhib﴾ (punishing). There is disagreement about borrowing such a form, namely a term used for something other than the verbal noun, like ﴿'ata'﴾ (gift), ﴿thawab﴾ (reward), ﴿'adhab﴾ (punishment), and ﴿kalam﴾ (speech). The Basrans do not permit it and do not analogize it.

Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and Nafi', in one variant from them, read ﴿withaqahu﴾ with a kasra on the waw. The majority read it with a fatha.

The one punished is the disbeliever in general. It was also said: he is Umayya ibn Khalaf. It was also said: Ubayy ibn Khalaf. It was also said: the intended meaning is Iblis, and the evidence has been established that he is more severely punished than people. This view is refuted by His saying: ﴿On that Day the human being will remember﴾, and all the pronouns are directed toward him.

When He, the Exalted, mentioned some of the conditions of those who are punished, He mentioned some of the conditions of the believer, saying: ﴿O soul at rest﴾. This address is apparently spoken by an angel. The majority read it with the feminine ta' (ya ayyatuha). Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿ya ayyuha﴾ without the ta'. I know of no one who said that it is masculine, even though the addressed noun is feminine, except the author of al-Badi'. This reading is evidence for that, and it has a basis in analogy: just as the dual and the plural are not inflected in the vocative, so the feminine is not inflected in the vocative of the feminine.

﴿Al-mutma'innah﴾ (at rest) means the secure one, who is not touched by fear or grief. Or it means the one who was at rest in the truth, whose heart was not mixed with doubt. Ibn Zayd said: it is said to her at the time of death and her departure from the body of the believer in this world. It was also said: at the time of resurrection. It was also said: at the time of entering Paradise.

﴿Ila rabbiki﴾ (to your Lord) means: to the appointed meeting with your Lord. It was also said: the "Lord" here is the human being, not the soul, meaning: enter into the bodies. The soul is a noun of genus. It was also said: this address is now directed to the believers. When He mentioned the state of the disbelievers, He said: O believers, persist and strive until you return pleased and well-pleasing. ﴿Radiyah﴾ (pleased) with what you have been given, ﴿mardiyyah﴾ (well-pleasing) in the sight of Allah.

﴿Fa-udkhuli fi 'ibadi﴾ means: enter among My righteous servants. ﴿Wa-udkhuli jannati﴾ (and enter My Paradise) along with them. It was also said: the soul and the spirit are meant, and the meaning is: enter the bodies of My servants.

The majority read ﴿fi 'ibadi﴾ in the plural. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, al-Dahhak, Mujahid, Abu Ja'far, Abu Salih, al-Kalbi, Abu Shaykh al-Hana'i, and al-Yamani read ﴿fi 'abdi﴾ in the singular. The more apparent view is that the noun of genus is intended, so its meaning and the meaning of the plural are the same. It was also said: there is an omission, and it addressed the soul in the singular, saying: "enter into My servant," meaning: into the body of My servant. The verb ﴿fa-udkhuli﴾ is transitive first with ﴿fi﴾ and second without a preposition. This is because, when the object of entering is not a real place, it is transitive with ﴿fi﴾: you enter into a matter and enter into the crowd of people. From this is His saying ﴿fa-udkhuli fi 'ibadi﴾. When the object of entering is a real place, it is generally transitive without the mediation of ﴿fi﴾.

It was said that this was revealed concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, and it was said concerning Hamza, and it was said concerning Khubayb ibn 'Adi, may Allah be pleased with them all.
